newsitem.title: USA: Slow Brazil loadings not seen aiding US soy sales.
newsitem.headline: Slow Brazil loadings not seen aiding US soy sales.

text.p: It is doubtful that buyers of Brazilian soybeans will turn to the United States just because of loading delays at Brazilian ports, U.S. analysts and grain exporters said.
Although occurring earlier than normal, analysts and exporters said loading delays are common in Brazil and buyers are prepared to have vessels wait in ports there.
"It happens every year," said one U.S. exporter. "We are just doing this 30 days ahead of normal."

Brazilian sources said exporters there sold soybeans earlier than usual this year in anticipation of an early harvest and to take advantage of high prices. As of Friday, 13 vessels were waiting in the Paranagua port to load soybeans or soymeal, but there was only enough material to load two or three, Brazilian shippers said.
"When it comes to Brazil, beans and meal are not really available in February and March," said Mickey Luth, grain analyst with the LaiFa Group.
Luth said only in situations of extreme need will a buyer cancel a Brazil purchase and come to the U.S.
"The world always seems to line up way too early for those soybeans," said Jerry Gidel, analyst with Dean Witter.
The delays have created some anxiety among U.S. soybean dealers because of the tight old-crop supply situation here.
"Right now the market will continue to be very nervous. We are extremely tight (on supplies)," said Gidel.

Gidel said the weekly U.S. soybean crush recently has been about a million bushels more than he had estimated. As a result, he estimated a 1996/97 soybean crush of 1.42 million bushels and ending stocks of 125 million.
Laifa's Luth said increases in exports and the soybean crush could cut ending stocks to 105 million to 110 million.
In its Feb 12 Supply/Demand Report, USDA estimated the 1996/97 crush at 1.41 million and ending stocks at 140 million.

Gidel said if his usage estimates are accurate, Chicago Board of Trade soybean futures could soon trade from $7.95 to $8.00 per bushel and soymeal near $265 per ton, possibly $280 if harvest delays persist in Brazil. CBOT March soybeans closed Friday at $7.83 a bushel and March soymeal at $257.60 a ton.
